p:
Thank you. We’re happy to see that, and I’m just happy for the record you’re letting folks know that. Early Learn has been around for a long time. There's 10,000 students

already in there perfecting the system, and the fact that the Council has built on extended day, extended year, I don’t think we get enough credit for that, and also the 2K expansion and creating the infrastructure and the framework for that work to happen. So the Council’s framework also calls for citywide multilingual outreach campaign to reach families with limited English proficiency in residents of shelters. What is in the current budget? Which languages are prioritized, and how will the administration measure whether underenrolled communities are being reached? Because I know your goal is 90,000 seats, but you only filled in 75. So, there’s still a gap. There’s still work to be done. Boots have to be on the ground to make sure we’re reaching families in underserved communities. We always see where they fill up really fast, but the communities that really need those seats have no clue that they exist. So how do we plan on closing that?

Yeah. You want me to take that? So, thank you for that, Council Member. So, the Division of Early Childhood Education works really closely with the Office of Student Enrollment which really they lead our

outreach efforts, and they are the brilliant minds behind My School and our admissions process through and through, not just early care and education, but even high school, which I am waiting for offers on Thursday for my daughter. And so we do a multi-media campaign. As you’ve even seen this year around. The mayor was involved inetnianlly doing PSAs in community and doing it in a way that is culturally-responsive to your point. And I know that you reached out asking that we do a– you know, provide targeted campaigns in a different language, and so I will admit that we will do better on that moving forward, but we do provide information mostly in print in all of the required languages that we are mandated to communicate in the communities and with families, and so we’ve been consistently providing that level of outreach. We’ve also been doing call campaigns, going into, again, shelters around other communities, providing information on how families can access the admissions and applications process. We had a treat truck out last week, near Tweed [sic] where I was personally handing out flyers and some treats. It was very fun. Encouraging, you know, families and people who walk by. I was really clear,

if you even know a three-year-old or four-year-old, take the flyer and encouraging them to sign up. But to your point, we can always do more. And so thank you for the investment and outreach, but there is a lot of work happening across the agency to make sure that we’re doing it in a way in languages in ways and in spaces that are culturally-response to communities, because to your point, there’s no point in having these seats if they remain unfilled. And so it is our commitment to make sure that we are out in community getting the word out.

And as we expand, what does student ratio look like in a classroom, very important. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Council Member. Next I want to call up Education Chair Dinowitz for his questions.
Thank you, Chair Gutiérrez. Feels good to say that, especially for such an important topic. I first need to ask what kind of treats were you giving out? We were just discussing.
You know–
Treats with a T, not trees?
Treats with a T, rice krispies.
Okay.
There was some hot cocoa.
Okay.
Some good stuff in there, and we let the littles pick as they passed by if they were, you know, with the adults in that moment.
Alright. So I won’t tell the Department of Health that you’re giving out that kind of candy instead of apples and carrots.
Oh, is this recorded?

On the record. I first want to say, I appreciate a lot of the conversation about the coordination with other agencies and even the framing of Early Childhood Education not as a program, but as something that uplifts families in our cities that we expect

universal child care to keep more young families in our city, reversing the high rates of out-migration that we see today for families with children under six, and Early Childhood Education is an incredibly important component. And I again, appreciate your vision that it is not about this particular program, but it’s part of a larger vision for our families. And I would just implore you that as you are having these interagency discussions doing this interagency group work, to recognize that housing is also a critical component of this. Families are leaving because we as a city are not building enough family-sized units, enough subsidized family-sized units. This is a constant fight where our city wants to build studios and maybe one-bedroom apartments, not enough two- and three-bedrooms. So, as part of our mission to support our families, I implore you as our Early Childhood team to support that mission as well. And Director Liss, I want to talk a little bit more about Early Intervention and not the transition of students who are receiving early intervention services to getting IESPs [sic], but ensuring that we are capturing all the students who need early intervention services. Can you walk us through the

process of the training you provide to teachers and families to recognize children who need early intervention services and what supports you provide to families to ensuring that they are applying for those services and receiving those services.

Sure. I can give a quick start, and I will say, we will make sure that for future hearings with the subcommittee we bring our Department of Health colleagues with us who are really the experts in administering this program. But we recognize that early intervention, you know, the whole point of if it is the earlier you start, the more support a family is able to receive and the stronger the trajectory for the child. The work of referring children to early intervention has to begin with their pediatricians, with medical professionals, with child care workers, with really any of the adults who are supporting and working with young children. And as we think about one of the potential benefits of universal child care and bringing more children into early care and education settings at an even younger age. Part of that benefit will be that they’ll be with trained educators who can recognize

the additional supports they need and refer them to those services.
But I want to be clear on my question. Are the early educators trained by DOE or the Mayor’s Office, DOHMH, to recognize the need for early intervention services?
Yeah.
Like, our educators specifically trained?

Thank you. In early– in 3k and Pre-K which is our template, we do provide training to providers in providing assessments that are early warning signs about a need for referral to special education, and in early intervention there are similar assessments. It’s called developmental monitoring that is done and we’ll be working with our partners at DOHMH on the potential roll out of developmental monitoring in 2K programs.
Can you talk a little bit more about that? That the teachers are benign trained by DOHMH to identify the need for an assessment.

So, the teachers are not necessarily being trained by DOHMH. What we have are Early Childhood educators who are coaches, hired by– in our employees of DECE. We have three levels of staff who support holistic coaching for not just the program leader, but also the classroom staff. And so we have social workers, instructional coordinators, and leadership coaches. They actually go into the program and provide tailored supports, and then we also have a second team of staff who support with– you know, that you’ve heard the Chancellor talk about MTSS, but you know, the tiered supports about how you know teachers and educators need to differentiate the way that they support our littles, right? And so what we do within the 40– within the first 45 days of a little attending is something called the ASQ. That is a screener. And so programs are required to do that, because it really is a snapshot into where that little might need additional support, and throughout their year, they also provide observations which go into another tool, which is our assessment tool, and our staff support again with those touch points, not just in-person, but maybe virtual to determine how we

can best support that child. But it does allow them to understand how to see early signs.

So, if I’m a parent who ends my kid to a 2K, a 2-Care program, I can be rest assured– like, look, I don’t know anything about early intervention, but I know that my child’s going to be screened, and that if they need early intervention services, that conversation will be?
Correct.

Okay. That's excellent. As this program builds out is critically important that we are capturing those students who need earlier intervention services so they either get their IESP and IEP early and they maybe they don’t need services by the time they get to, you know, high school. Right? That's the goal is to make sure kids are getting the support they need as early as possible. And then my second question is what work are you doing I guess collaboratively to ensure that there are enough teachers, and as you expand these programs, you have enough early education– Early Childhood educators to meet the growing demand for Early Childhood Education?

Absolutely. We know this is going to be a huge area we have to focus on in terms of building out the pipeline of new people to bring them into early care and education, and then supporting our current workforce to ensure that they are able to sustain themselves and able to grow and remain in the field as professionals. So, as I referenced, we are planning to bring and we’re kicking off actually this week, a group with all agencies in the city who in any way or another touch workforce development so that we can think much more comprehensively about how we do this work. We’ll be partnering with institutions of higher education to understand what are some of the barriers that folks face coming into these programs and how can we take those barriers away, whether it’s the time that classes are offered, the language, the cost, and address those pieces. We also want to think about earlier exposure to early care and education as a professional field, potentially working through some of our pathways programs and partnering to make sure that young people who are thinking about professions, recognize that this a real career path. Of course, in

all of this we recognize that if we want to bring more people into the field, as Chair Gutiérrez touched on, we have to address the compensation and longterm career path for folks who come into this work. So, while we’re building out a pipeline and encourage more folks to participate in making it easier to participate, we also have to make this more attractable, sustainable field.

Yeah, I would imagine a world where high school kids have that early childhood care in their schools and they become inspired to go to college for it, but it also needs that support. So I’m pleased to hear about what that workforce– that that work is beginning. I think CUNY can be a great partner. I myself was a New York City teaching fellow and I got into this profession with a subsidized master’s degree– or that profession. I’m in a different profession now, aren’t I? But it was that sort of, you know, support that I might– my cohort got for our master’s degrees that allowed us to enter the profession, and I would love to see more of that through– whether it’s through our CUNY system or the workforce development program, creating the lowest barrier to entry. So high-quality, qualified

people who care about our littles, as you call them. I thik it’s adorable. I love it. So, can get into this– the profession where we will so desperately need more Early Childhood educators. Thank you so much, Director and DC Hawkins, and thank you, Chair. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much, Chair Dinowitz. I want to just recognize Council Member Felder is on Zoom or was on Zoom. Thank you for joining us. Next we’re going to have Council Member Restler ask questions followed by Council Member Brewer.

Thank you so much, Chair Gutiérrez. I really appreciate the opportunity to ask a few questions, and thank you for the thoughtful testimony today, Director Liss. What do you think is the target 3K capacity per district? We saw about a third of school districts this current year had more than 90 percent of their seats field, which such a tight vacancy rate makes it really hard for families to find a seat locally. We know when you’ve got a three-year-old, you’re not traveling from, you know, one side of a school district to another or to another school district altogether. Do you have a suggested benchmark of what we should be

looking at, or for Deputy Chancellor Hawkins, as well?
I know you posed this question to me before, Council Member, and I–
[interposing] I’m consistent if anything.

And I appreciate that, but I’m going to unfortunately have to get back to you on that. And really wanting to be thoughtful on developing those metrics alongside ED Liss to make sure we’re being thoughtful. But I will share this, just for you to know, and for others in the space. For the current school year we have 51,924 3K seats, and capac– and utilization for the year as of our last check last week is around 84 percent. And this is pretty much flat to where we were this time last year, or rather at the end of last year. And so wanting to be thoughtful about that 84-85 percent utilization and making sure that every seat is filled, but also that communities can remain nimble enough to meet the growing and changing need in their communities as we welcome additional three-year-olds.
So, is that– just so my math is right, 42-43,000 kids in our 3K schools.
That’s right.

So, great. As we look toward the next school year, you know, we saw a significant– a healthy reduction in the number of extended day 3K seats from the Adams administration. The data I’m looking at is from about 5,250 down to 4,869. We know that low-income families need extended day seats the most, and yet, we see higher rates of occupancy– utilization is probably the right word– of seats in our school-based system than in our CBO system where we have the extended day seats available. Are you looking at revisiting that distribution of extended day seats? Are you hoping to expand the number of extended day seats for the next school year?

So, I think 2K is a step in that direction of recognizing that families need extended day, but also, you know, non-means-tested seats, and many of our extended day seats right now– and we are very grateful for it– is subsidized partially with CCBG funds, and so we have

to follow the Child Care Assistance process or application process that determines eligibility based on, you know, a host of criterion. And so what we are looking at meeting that need based off, you know, caregiver feedback, but also our providers. They are saying that it’s just more profitable if done right for them to provide an extended day and extended year model, and so we are doing that with City Tax Levy and 2K is an example of us doing that.

Yeah, I understand. We’ve seen a decline in our enrollment in our Department of Education now for a number of years, seven, eight-plus years, healthy and significant decline that we need to reverse, and the expansion of our Early Childhood Education system directly connected to our DOE schools represents an opportunity for us to build that pipeline back up, and I– you would not be doing your jobs if you weren’t thinking about how to do that effectively, and that is an incredibly important priority. The same time, the extended day seats at our CBOs, it think, are being underutilized and we haven’t been sending families there or guiding families there as much as I think we could when those are the seats

that would be most beneficial to families. So, I do feel like there is a calibration in the previous administration that was not right, that we need to revisit, and I hope that as you look to see distribution for the next school year, that that’s a topic that you’re going to give a hard look at.

Can I– I want to jump in with one thing on this. I know we’ve talked about this in the past which is that those extended day newer seats, as Deputy Chancellor Hawkins just mentioned, do all come with means testing which as we continue to expand the system, our goal is to create new seats and programs that are universally accessible that do not require families to go through that level of onerous burdensome–
[interposing] Yeah.

application process. That said, while we continue to have seats in our system that are funded through funding streams that require that. It is really incumbent on us to think about how we support families through that process. I know you focus on outreach and some of the prior questions, other Council Members did as

well. We need to rebuild the work of direct family outreach and engagement–
[interposing] Yep.

to help families through that process. And as we think about what it would take to fill those seats and programs, we know that families need support to navigate that process, because it is burdensome and requires them to complete quite a lot of paperwork.
Totally, totally–
[interposing] All to say, I think filling those seats is quite connected to our outreach work.

Yeah. And in two months there’s only so much outreach you can do. This is an effort that takes a lot more and I’m sure our numbers aren’t where we want them to be for this coming school year, but hopefully there’ll be ongoing outreach efforts.
Absolutely.

Can I do two more quick questions, is that okay? Fast. I’m on

it. Quick questions, mostly germane. How are you making determinations on new sites? I know that I’ve raised a couple opportunities in District 33 such as northern Greenpoint, 274 Atlantic as examples that we really hope to see activated for Early Childhood next year. If you could keep us posted. What’s the kind of– how are you thinking about that? And secondly, we’ve got a 16,000-ish wait list for our child care vouchers right now for families that really need these vouchers. We have enough money to keep everyone who has a voucher in a voucher for next year, but we have zero dollars associated with that wait list. Any thoughts there. And then thirdly, which this is neither of your responsibilities, but we see child care centers shut down in our district all the time. I assume for good reason, for the most part. The Health Department is doing its best to try to ensure that our kids are in safe places. There’s nothing more important, but then it’s an entirely opaque process of what happens from there. We get no information from the Health Department. We– we’ll email the Commissioner, the Deputy Commissioner, and 17 people under the Deputy Commissioner. I know all of them, and they all give me very little information

and it’s incredibly frustrating. Simone, maybe you can go– Deputy Chancellor, maybe you want to go back to the Health Department and help there, too. But the– but in all seriousness, can you please help us so that when there are corrective action plans, that information is getting to our offices. We can work together, inform families, try to push and support providers to get the information submitted that’s needed so that we don’t have daycares closed in our communities for weeks on end? With a– so, I know it’s neither of your– it’s not– this is not germane to the hearing, but it’s frustrating me to no end.

I’ll go very quickly. And I’ll just give a shout out to our Health Department partners. They work really hard, and we can work together to get you that information, Council Member. And so really quickly on the city-owner lease, shout out to you and Council Member Brewer and others for raising this issue up I think at the start of my tenure. We are looking at, you know, community needs, and that has since changed since these buildings were put online, and so we want to work really closely with you. W’ere looking at independent providers in communities as well, because

we don’t want to oversaturate neighborhoods and have the unintended consequences of putting businesses out of business. And so we want to look at what the community needs in concert with all of you and then hopefully based on those needs put those buildings online at a rate that makes most sense.

And as to your question for the voucher waiting list. This is something that we’re continuing to look at, continuing to talk with our partners in Albany about– because we do recognize that there are many, many families who are waiting and it impacts not only the families but the providers who serve them.
Would you be willing to work with us and the Health Department to try to improve that process?
Yes, would love to have a separate conversation with you and the–
[interposing] Thank you.
Health Department on that.

THank you, Chair.

CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Council Member Restler. I want to acknowledge we’ve been joined by Council Member Pierina Sanchez, and next up for questions, Council Member Brewer.

Thank you, and I want to thank Deputy Chancellor Hawkins for calling me about these empty centers. So how many are left that are vacant? I know the ones that are filled. Rita’s [sic] is filled. I think Rethmine [sp?].
27 to be filled?
Yes.
Aye, aye, aye.
And we’re working to create plans for all of those, and that number has decreased since I started. We have repurposed, and so we are working to get that number down.

Okay. The folks at the School Construction Authority didn’t know that nobody knew about it, but I corrected them. The zero to two, I have a question about that. When I talked to Health Department, 219 72 Broadway, they actually on the second floor I believe found opportunities for

three classrooms to be zero to two. So, how does– can one be on the second floor? How does that work, or do you need to change that? What’s the status? In the past, because I’ve been doing this daycare work since 1970-something. It had to be on the first floor.
So, infants are required to be on the first or ground floor. That is codified in Article 47 of the Health Code. however, preschool-aged children, so those two and above can be up–
[interposing] No, I’m talking about the zero to two, the infants.
So, infants cannot be above the ground floor, Council Member.
Okay. Is that– should that be changed? Are you going to have enough first floor?

So, that’s something as we build out our infant work, which we hope, you know, happens after we really, you know, solidify our toddler, two-year-old programming. It’s something we will have to look at. Because we want–

you know, child safety is paramount, and the Health Code–
[interposing] No, I know.
you know, has that as a reason, but that’s something we’re going to look into.

And I would just add, I know this has been a topic, a hot topic for many years, and the restriction as Deputy Chancellor is really to make sure that in an emergency that provider could evacuate with children who are not yet able to walk. There are pathways for providers who are able to demonstrate safety plans for them to be able to explore other spaces. And we want to make sure that for providers it’s clear how they can do that, but the– broadly we do not– we do not plan to do anything that would in any way imperil health and safety.

No, I understand that. I’m just saying I think we’re on the second floor, but I can double check, and it was okay. Just so you know. Number two, after school, can you explain– I know the nonprofit sector has more of an

opportunity than DOE. Can you just explain generally how you’re going to collaborate between the programs and after school, because that’s the call that I get all the time. Won’t go to this program because it doesn’t have all-day. How many have all-day? How may don’t? How are you looking at this, and is there funding?

So, for 3K and Pre-K programs, we’ll just note that many programs that are offered in a community-based organization setting, some do have extended day programs like those that Council Member Restler was referencing.
Yes.
That are– you know, for subsidized. Others may have programs where the family can pay a fee for after school. Similarly, many of our public school programs have on-site after school providers. Some–
[interposing] Will those–
[interposing] Some may be available to three and four-year-olds, but not all. A number of programs are permitted just to serve children in kindergarten and up.
That’s my experience.
Yep.
And so are you thinking, though, to try to get more funding for the after school for the smaller children? Is that on your radar?
It is on our radar, yes. And 2K we are right now anticipating for it to be a full-day program, and extended day program. And so we are looking at additional models like that, Council Member.

Okay. The other issue is the Bright Horizons, that was one that closed. How many are for-profit in your portfolio? I’m not decrying the fact that it closed. There were a lot of issues there. But how many are for-profit? How– that’s what I want to know in your portfolio.
So, I think we’ll have to get back to you on that number, Council Member. The how many are for-profit?

Yes. I’m not always supportive of them, so I just wanted to know what the number is. I’m not talking about ones that

are on place like at a corporation, but ones that in the community for profit. This group seemed to have a lot of problems.
We’ll get back to you on that.

Okay. And the other thing is, people are asking me– I assume this happens, but are there public notices at the community-based organizations so that parents know what their rights are for services and assessments? Is that something that already exists or should it exist? In other words, do parents get that information? I guess it could be up on the wall or other kinds of communication.

I will say, as a current Pre-K parent, I receive quite a lot of information from my child’s program about different services that we might be eligible for. The developmental screenings that were referenced, you know, and any basic–
And you were at a CBO, not at a DOE?
I’m at a DOE school.
Okay.
But the same communications are shared with all families and all programs.
Even at the CBOs. some parents think not, I’m just telling you.
I think we can always do more to improve how information gets to families, and we can keep working on that.

I’m just telling you. And then quickly, the centers that end up with, you know, public health hazards from Department of Health– and I really have, like you, I have a lot of respect for the Department of Health and the work they do. It’s incredibly important. But do you know how are they handled? Are they told to the parents? Obviously, in the past, there have been issues around these lines. How does that information get transplanted to parents when there’s a Department of Health and how does it get reinspected?

So, when there is a closure at a child care program, if there’s– so stepping back. Child care programs may receive

violations that are not significant enough to merit a closure–
[interposing] Correct.

and the provider is able to remedy that. All information about past violations at child care sites is available to families and we are reinstating the performance summary cards that providers have to post in their window that include information about their inspection history. When there is a significant enough violation that it leads to a closure, all parents in the program are notified, and then as the program is reinspected and is able to demonstrate that they have corrected the issue and then are able to safely reopen, that information is shared with–

[interposing] I mean, I hear you. I’m just– parents are concerned, and so I would think that would be the norm, but obviously parents think otherwise. And just finally, the CEC, I go to all the meetings. Do you think there should be– obviously, we have special ed, we have ELL, we have parents. Do you think there should be a preschool parent on that CEC in addition?
I love your thinking. We’re in active discussions with the Chancellor about that very thing.

Okay. Thank you very much. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much, Council Member Brewer. I think we– there [inaudible]. Okay, great. So sorry. So I’m going to continue asking some questions. Great. I wanted to ask on– back to 2-Care. I made a note. Okay. so, in your testimony, we’re anticipating 2,000 students ages zero to two.
Age two. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Age two, excuse me.

Yes. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: For the fall, okay. What will that look like? I guess this is considered year one. Can you just walk us through what it would look like years two, three, and four, at least through the end of the first administration to expand the program or, yeah, continue to invest in it. Just kind of walk us through what that means.

Absolutely. So, the Governor’s funding commitment that she announced earlier this year that I know many folks including yourself [inaudible] referenced includes $73 million for this school year which will allow us to serve about 2,000 children, and then that funding level from the state increases to $425 million in the following year, and we have a target of serving about 12,000 children. In terms of sort of specific targets for years three and four, I think we really want to assess how many children actually participate in the program, what does family uptake look like, as we work with providers to understand their capacity to offer 2K and recognize we’ll need to continue building out capacity. I think we want to look at what that progression looks like to then determine, you know, specific enrollment targets for years three and four, but the goal is as I said to be serving every two-year-old who wants to participate in the program by the end of the first term. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. So you don’t have a sense of how many 2-Care seats will be contracted seats since it’s early.

I think we want to be– we want to be responsive to family need, and to-date, no one has ever gone out and comprehensively asked every family in the city would you participate if this program were available to you? And so part of what we have to do is over this year is really do that family engagement, so we know what we’re building toward. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: And then I know the RFEI, right, that’s what– just closed on Friday. I just want to make sure I’m using the right term. I know it just closed on Friday. Do you have any preliminary numbers, at least like how many responses you got?

None that would be responsible to share those with you now, but I promise to round back and give you the correct numbers. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. And can you just confirm, the responses for the RFEI are mandated to be all in English?

Yes. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. Is there– I guess maybe depending on the feedback, and these

were just separate conversations that we’ve had regarding the ongoing RFP. Have there been conversations about language access for the responses for the RFPs? I know– can you just confirm if the language in the– any of the RFPs from the Department are in any other language besides English?

So, it’s my understanding city at large, any form of procurement process must be in English, but any additional information that we give in like info sessions, documents that we created for folks to understand that this is an opportunity they can access was translated into other languages, but the actual mechanism, the RFI had to be English. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, and the responses are in English. Okay. Well, I don’t know– I look forward to maybe having that conversation with the administration that some of the feedback that we have gotten in the past about the ability for some providers to not really be able to either respond fully or just, like, you know, just an obvious challenge is the language barrier and then having to kind of out-source folks to help them fill it out. So, I understand that, but would love to kind of have

that conversation with you all. Can you share what criteria the DOE and the office is using to determine which neighborhoods to targets for seats in the first year of 2-Care?

We’re looking at a couple of different criteria as we think about which parts of the city we’ll start with. Looking at family need both in terms of their overall economic need and a lack of availability of subsidized or low-cost child care. So, looking at where we have large numbers of two-year-olds who are both, you know, facing high rates of child poverty and don’t necessarily have that access of care today. We’re also looking at provider capacity, recognizing the quick timeline we’re on for this first year. We want to start in places where providers are ready and able to participate. At the same time, we know that we have to do work citywide to build out child care capacity in communities that don’t yet have that as fully. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: And how are you all thinking how the application process will work? Will it look like 3K, Pre-K, the same schools .gov website?

It will look similarly. We’re working through with partners in the Office of Student Enrollment, all the particular policies to be able to share that with families in coming weeks and months. But yes, it will be a centralized enrollment process. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: And I’m not sure if My City will continue into this administration, but is that something you’re all thinking of working the 2-Care application process into the My City app, or– again, I have no idea what’s going on with it, but I’m just asking.

So, currently the My City portal is sort of the pathway for all of our means-tested child care programs, and so for families who are applying for vouchers and going through that eligibility determination process, that goes through My City. Currently, we will be looking at how to, you know, make sure that families understand what the right door is to go into for 2K, but also making sure that families have no wrong door. So, if a family logs onto My Schools or My City, thinking that that might be where they find 2K,
